stories.headline: White House replaces national cyber director after a week of tech outages
stories.summary: Sean Cairncross is out as White House national cyber director, days after outages disrupted air travel, banking and government systems. Kirsten Davies, the Pentagon's chief information officer, will fill the job in an acting capacity. Outlets differ on whether he was fired or is leaving.
stories.why_it_matters: The office coordinates federal cybersecurity policy, and the change comes while travelers, bank customers and federal agencies are still dealing with a run of outages whose causes have not been fully explained.
stories.background: The national cyber director advises the president on cybersecurity and coordinates policy across federal agencies. President Trump named Cairncross, then a Republican National Committee executive, to the post in February 2025. Over the past week, outages hit Microsoft services, flights, banks and a National Security Agency network. Microsoft said it had no indication its outage was related to the Federal Aviation Administration's nationwide ground stop. Davies comes to the role from the Defense Department, where she is chief information officer.

facts.text: Sean Cairncross is leaving the post of White House national cyber director, a White House official told CBS News.
Kirsten Davies, the Pentagon's chief information officer, will take over the role in an acting capacity.
The change came days after technology outages disrupted US air travel, banking and national security systems, according to Reuters reporting carried by other outlets.
The National Security Agency saw a third day of disruptions to its internal network, NSA Net, on Thursday, the Guardian reported.
Microsoft said it had no indication that the FAA's nationwide ground stop was related to its services.
Trump named Cairncross, a Republican National Committee executive, as national cyber director in February 2025.

He "will be leaving his position," a White House official told CBS News; other outlets say he is being replaced.

stories.headline: Senate passes bipartisan permitting overhaul 62-33, sending it to the House
stories.summary: The Senate voted 62-33 Thursday night for a bill that would speed federal permitting reviews for energy and infrastructure projects and limit legal challenges to them. Thirty-one Democrats and two Republicans voted no. The bill now needs House approval before going to President Trump.
stories.why_it_matters: Supporters say faster approvals for power plants and transmission lines would raise energy supply and lower bills, and the bill would make data centers pay for the energy they use; opponents say it weakens environmental review of projects near where people live.
stories.background: Building a power line, pipeline or power plant in the US often requires years of federal environmental review and can be held up by lawsuits. Lawmakers from both parties have tried for years to shorten that process, and electricity demand from artificial intelligence data centers has added pressure. The bill, called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, cleared a first procedural vote 73-25 on Nov. 9. Democrats split over it, with environmental groups opposed.

facts.text: The Senate passed the bill 62-33 on Thursday night.
Thirty-one Democrats and two Republicans voted against it.
The bill would speed environmental reviews, expand the electric grid and limit legal challenges to projects.
It includes provisions meant to make data centers pay for the energy they use.
The bill must still pass the House before going to President Trump.
Many Democrats and environmental groups opposed the bill.
The bill cleared its first procedural vote in the Senate 73-25 on Nov. 9.

stories.headline: Senate Republicans block a resolution to end the Iran war in first vote since the midterms
stories.summary: Senate Republicans on Thursday blocked a war powers resolution that would have directed President Trump to end hostilities with Iran. Democrats and a small number of Republicans supported it. Democrats, who are set to take control of both chambers, have not settled on a plan for what they will do next.
stories.why_it_matters: The vote leaves the president free to continue the war without new limits from Congress, at least until the new Congress is seated.
stories.background: The US has been at war with Iran this year, and Congress has voted several times on whether to order an end to it under the War Powers Resolution, a law meant to limit military action without congressional approval. The Senate rejected one such measure 47-53 in March and approved one for the first time in June. Republicans lost seats in this month's midterm elections, and Democrats are set to hold majorities in the House and Senate. Sen. Tim Kaine, a Virginia Democrat, has been a lead sponsor of these efforts.

facts.text: Senate Republicans blocked a measure Thursday that would have directed President Trump to end hostilities in Iran.
It was the Senate's first vote on the conflict since the midterm elections.
Some Republicans joined Democrats in support, but the Washington Times reported there was no new Republican support compared with earlier votes.
Democrats are set to take House and Senate majorities, and some want to press the administration to end the war, though CBS News reported the exact plan is not clear.
The Senate rejected an Iran war powers resolution 47-53 in March.
In June the Senate approved a war powers resolution on Iran for the first time.

stories.headline: Justice Department moves to drop its lawsuit over Alaska's Senate race after Peltola's win
stories.summary: The Justice Department asked a federal appeals court Thursday to dismiss the lawsuit it filed before the election seeking to block certification of Alaska's US Senate race if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan lost. Democrat Mary Peltola won the race this week.
stories.why_it_matters: The filing removes a federal legal challenge to seating the winner of a Senate election, in a case that tested whether Washington can hold up a state's certified results.
stories.background: Alaska's Senate race pitted incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan against Democrat Mary Peltola. A second candidate, a retired teacher also named Dan Sullivan, was on the ballot, and the Justice Department sued less than two weeks before the election, asking for an investigation into whether votes for him were meant for the senator. US District Judge Sharon Gleason dismissed the suit on Nov. 1, and the department filed notice that it would appeal. Peltola was declared the winner this week.

facts.text: In a filing Thursday, the Trump administration asked a federal appeals court to dismiss the lawsuit it filed before the midterm elections.
The suit had sought to block certification of the results if Sen. Dan Sullivan lost.
Democrat Mary Peltola won the race.
The case centered on a second candidate who shared the senator's name.

US District Judge Sharon Gleason dismissed the lawsuit before the election, writing that the Constitution gives states the authority to run elections; the Justice Department then filed a notice of appeal.

framing.note: Says the department "gives up" and notes critics called the suit meritless.

stories.headline: Trump's nominee to lead CISA declines to say who won in 2020 or call Jan. 6 an attack
stories.summary: Michael LoSapio, nominated to lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, told senators Thursday he does not consider the Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol riot an "attack" and would not say who won the 2020 presidential election. He said he would reevaluate the agency's budget and staffing if confirmed.
stories.why_it_matters: CISA helps states protect election systems and helps defend power, water and other critical networks, so its director's views on past elections and on the agency's size bear on how that work is done.
stories.background: CISA is the Department of Homeland Security agency responsible for defending critical infrastructure and supporting election security. LoSapio is the chief information security officer at Palantir, a data-analytics company. He appeared before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, where Sen. Richard Blumenthal, a Connecticut Democrat, questioned him about the 2020 election and Jan. 6. The hearing came during a week of major technology outages.

facts.text: LoSapio said the Jan. 6, 2021, riot at the Capitol was not an "attack" when pressed by Sen. Richard Blumenthal.
He did not answer who won the 2020 presidential election.
He told lawmakers he plans to reevaluate CISA's budget and staffing if confirmed.
Trump chose Palantir's chief information security officer to lead CISA.
Some people in the cybersecurity industry have raised concerns about the nomination, Nextgov reported before the hearing.

framing.note: Says he "rejects" Jan. 6 as an attack, a more active verb than declining to answer.
Says he "ducks" questions and itself calls Jan. 6 the "Capitol attack."

stories.headline: Army postpones detonation of 5 tons of unstable explosive in Iowa after safety concerns
stories.summary: The Army postponed Friday's planned detonation of about 5 tons of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown after residents and lawmakers raised concerns about a plume of lead dust. The BBC reported the blast is now set for Monday.
stories.why_it_matters: People near the plant had been asked to leave their homes, and the Army itself expects the blast to send lead-bearing dust into the air over parts of Iowa and possibly Illinois.
stories.background: Lead azide is an explosive used in making munitions. The Army says 68 drums of it at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant have degraded, cannot be used and could explode if moved, so it plans to destroy them in controlled detonations. The Environmental Protection Agency permitted the operation, according to the Army. Residents of nearby Middletown were asked to evacuate temporarily, and Iowa lawmakers said they were given short notice.

facts.text: The Army delayed the detonation of about 5 tons of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant.
Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle announced the postponement after lawmakers said they were given short notice.

The Army had asked Middletown residents to evacuate temporarily on Friday before detonating 68 drums of the chemical.
The material is unusable and might explode if moved, and residents worry a lead dust cloud could cause contamination and health problems.
The dust plume could spread across parts of Iowa and Illinois.
The Army's advisory had scheduled two controlled detonations for about noon on Nov. 20 and said the EPA permitted the operation.

positions.claim: The Army cited a drop in temperature, Fox News reported.
The delay followed concerns from residents and pleas from Iowa lawmakers, with the Army saying public safety is its top priority.

stories.headline: Judge rules agriculture secretary's religious emails to staff violated the First Amendment
stories.summary: A federal judge ruled that Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins's religious emails to about 100,000 department employees were unconstitutional and ordered limits on such messages. The department said it may challenge the ruling, the Guardian reported.
stories.why_it_matters: The ruling sets a limit on how far a Cabinet official can go in promoting a religion to the federal workers she supervises. In today's ingest it was covered mostly by left-leaning outlets, with one right-leaning outlet.
stories.background: Rollins leads the US Department of Agriculture. A federal employees' union and department workers sued, saying her holiday messages to staff, including at Easter and Christmas, had become increasingly proselytizing and violated the First Amendment's ban on government establishment of religion. The case, National Federation of Federal Employees v. USDA, was filed in federal court in Northern California. The judge has now sided with the employees.

facts.text: A federal judge ruled that Rollins's religious emails to 100,000 employees were unconstitutional.
The judge ordered limits on Rollins's promotion of her religious beliefs to the department, saying the emails violated the First Amendment.
The messages at issue included Christmas and Easter emails.
The department said it may challenge the ruling, according to the Guardian.
Federal employees sued the department over the emails, arguing they violated the First Amendment's establishment clause.
